\section{ABM Results: The Broker's Advantage in a Simulated Matching Market}

\subsection{Model and methods}

To formalize and illustrate the theory developed in this article, this
section describes an ABM of brokerage in a general matching market and
presents the results of exploratory computational simulations. Their
purpose is not to prove or disprove the theory, but to operationalize
it, explore the dynamics it entails while providing concrete
illustrations to the reader, and generate falsifiable propositions that
future empirical work can use as hypotheses.

The theory makes claims about trajectories and feedback among
heterogeneous, boundedly informed actors interacting repeatedly, making
the ABM a natural tool to make its mechanisms explicit and sharpen its
propositions.

The model is domain-agnostic and represents any market in which a broker
facilitates pairwise matches and accumulates cross-market data from
doing so. All agents use heuristic decision rules, and no agent is
perfectly rational. One period equals one full update of the simulation
loop; each period could be taken to represent one calendar month, one
week, or one day, for instance, depending on the pace of the market that
one wants to represent.

Pseudo-code and complete specifications for the model are included as
\textbf{Appendix A and B}, respectively, and the code base for the project,
implemented in Julia, is publicly available at
\texttt{https://github.com/m-laprise/brokerage-abm}. It includes the
scripts needed to reproduce the experiments that generated the data
analyzed in this section, extract every number mentioned, create the
figures and tables, and generate the results section in its entirety.

\emph{Setup}. Many principals and a single broker, connected through an
undirected network, inhabit the market. Each period, a principal draws a
demand for new pairwise matches. Principals seeking matches search on
their own for counterparties (self-search channel) or outsource to the
broker (broker channel). The decision is made by comparing a running
satisfaction score for each channel; principals who have never used the
broker rely on its reputation (average satisfaction of current clients).
After each period, each agent exits with probability $\eta$ and is
replaced by a fresh entrant.

The schematic below summarizes initialization and the within-period sequence;
the mechanisms are described in detail afterward.

\begin{center}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figs/model_overview.pdf}
\begin{minipage}{0.96\linewidth}
\small\textbf{Model overview.} Initialization creates the period-0 market
state. Each period, principals choose a search channel, eligible prediction

recorded before turnover, after which the next period begins.
\end{minipage}
\end{center}

\emph{Nature of the matching problem} (Appendix B \S2). Each principal has a
fixed type, a vector of observable characteristics. A realized match
between two principals yields an output equal to a fixed function of the
two parties' types plus noise. The signal is unknown to everyone and
must be learned. It has two parts, combined by a mixing weight $\rho$. The
first is a general-quality term computed as the average of the two
parties' quality scores, which depend on their type alone: a
high-quality agent is high-quality for everyone. The second is a
complementarity term that depends on the interaction of the two types:
even two high-quality agents can make a bad match. At $\rho=1$ match value
is pure general quality, at $\rho=0$ it is pure complementarity.

\emph{Complexity of the matching problem} (Appendix B \S2c). A gain $\delta$
sets how complex the prediction problem is by modulating the
complementarity term up or down by a fixed amount depending on which of
two regions of type-pair space a pair falls into, with the regions
constructed to add structure to the problem. The effect is to raise the
number of independent components needed to describe how match value
varies across pairs. The gain $\delta$ acts only on the complementarity term
and has no effect at $\rho=1$, where match value is pure general quality.

\emph{Data collection and learning} (Appendix A \S3, algorithms 2 and 3;
Appendix B \S3). Principals record their own match history, with the type
of each partner and the realized output of the pairing, brokered or not.
The broker records the matches it mediates, with the type of both
parties and the realized outputs, across all clients. Principals and the
broker each fit a small neural network to their data using gradient
descent, to learn to predict match output. At every period for the
broker, and every other period for the principals, agents train on
observations from the recent past to update their prediction function.
To respect the symmetry of the unordered pairs in its training data, the
broker uses as input a symmetric feature vector built from the type
vectors.

As a robustness experiment, I repeat the complete design with Ridge regression
replacing both neural networks. Principals regress output on the candidate's
type; the broker uses the same symmetric additive and bilinear pair features as
in the main model. Histories, training window, observation cap, fitting cadence,
and reporting seeds are unchanged. Baseline calibration on 10 seeds excluded
from reporting selected $\lambda_a=0.003$ for principals and
$\lambda_b=0.001$ for the broker. This tests whether neural-network flexibility
is necessary for the broker's ranking advantage; it does not equalize the
learners' data or feature representations.

\emph{Search and match formation} (Appendix B \S\S6--7). Self-search draws on
known network neighbors and a small random pool of strangers; brokered
search, on the broker's standing roster and current clients. Agents use
their prediction functions to rank potential candidates and offers are
made to the top ones. For known partners, principals use the mean of
their past experiences with them as the predicted value. Offers above
the reservation threshold are accepted. When a match is made, its output
is realized and both parties form a direct tie. Ties persist until one
of the agents exits.

\emph{Economics} (Appendix B \S4). A match's realized output is its per-period
value to each party. All quantities (reservation threshold, fees, search
costs) are in common monetary units and are calibrated relative to the
average match output over many random pairs. Every agent shares a
reservation threshold (or outside option): offers are made or accepted
only when predicted outputs exceed it. Self-search has a cost for each
requested position whether filled or not, whereas the broker's fee is
charged only on successful placements; both are an equal amount.
Satisfaction scores net out costs or fees.

These modeling choices are the formal counterpart of the theoretical
claims made above. Decomposing match output into general-quality and
complementarity separates the attributional channel from the relational
one. A principal learns from its own one-sided history, while the broker
learns from both sides of matches and pools across clients.

\emph{Measurement} (Appendix B \S8). Diagnostic measures are recorded every
period. In this article, structural position is measured as the broker's
betweenness centrality in the graph, that is, the share of shortest
paths between principals that run through the broker (Brandes 2001;
Freeman 1977), as the standard \emph{whole-network} measure of brokerage
potential. The results would be substantively similar if examining the
ego-network measures of Burt's constraint and effective size (Borgatti
1997; Burt 1992; Everett and Borgatti 2020); an alternative set of
figures to that effect is included as Supplementary Material. The access
fraction is the share of standard brokered matches in which the
counterparty was not already tied to the demander. Prediction quality is
measured on deterministic random-partner holdout samples evaluated
against noiseless true output: Spearman rank correlation measures
whether predictions order possible matches correctly, while $R^2$
measures level accuracy; gaps subtract the principal value from the
broker value. $R^2$ varies much more because its finite-holdout denominator
is realized-output variance, so modest prediction errors can produce extreme
negative values when that variance is small. This volatility does not affect
model behavior or the conclusions based on ranking, matching, and realized
output because $R^2$ is diagnostic only and never enters a decision rule.

\emph{Results}. All results are computed from a parameter sweep of the
simulated market. In the baseline regime,
$N=1{,}000$ agents interact for $T=500$ periods with matching-function parameters
$\rho=0.5$ and $\delta=0.5$, turnover $\eta=0.02$, reservation threshold $f_r=0.6$,
initial network degree $k_G=6$, broker roster share $\alpha_R=0.2$, and
self-search pool size $n_{\mathrm{strangers}}=10$. The simulation retains all
periods, but time-series displays begin at $t=30$ to omit the initialization
transient. This display cutoff does not change the simulation or the late-period
estimands. Around this baseline, I vary one parameter at a time
($\rho\in\{0,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.85,1\}$, $\eta\in\{0,0.001,0.01,0.02,0.03\}$,
$N\in\{500,1000,1500\}$, $f_r\in\{0.4,0.6,0.9,1.2\}$,
$\delta\in\{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1\}$, $k_G\in\{4,12\}$,
$\alpha_R\in\{0.1,0.2,0.4\}$, and
$n_{\mathrm{strangers}}\in\{0,10,50\}$) and I sweep eight two-parameter
grids: the six pairwise combinations of $\{\rho,\eta,N,f_r\}$ and the
$\rho\times\delta$ grid over their full one-at-a-time levels, plus a focused
$\rho\times f_r$ refinement over
$\rho\in\{0.7,0.85,1\}$ and $f_r\in\{0.9,1.05,1.2\}$. In the six general grids,
$\rho\times\eta$ and $\rho\times N$ use $\rho\in\{0,0.5,0.85,1\}$,
$\rho\times f_r$ uses $\rho\in\{0,0.5,1\}$, and the remaining axes reuse their
one-at-a-time levels. The design comprises \pv{nRegimes} regimes, with
\pv{nGeneralSeeds} independent seeds generally and
\pv{nBaselineSeeds} at the baseline (\pv{nRuns} runs in total). Reported statistics are
ensemble means over seeds, summarized by time averages over fixed windows within a
run: late means over the final 20 periods ($t\in[481,500]$), used for all reported
levels unless noted otherwise, and early means over $t\in[50,70]$, to quantify
within-run drift. Full parameter values are given in Appendix~B~\S10.
Monte Carlo convergence was assessed by comparing estimates from the first 10
seeds with all 20 seeds generally, and the first 20 with all 50 seeds at the
baseline, and by computing Student-$t$ 95\% intervals from seed-level
late-window means. Across the \pv{mcOutcomeCount} non-$R^2$ outcomes shown in
the figures, median relative interval half-widths across conditions ranged from
\pv{mcCiMedianMinPercent}\% to \pv{mcCiMedianMaxPercent}\%; median relative
nested-seed changes ranged from \pv{mcNestedMedianMinPercent}\% to
\pv{mcNestedMedianMaxPercent}\%. Relative precision uses the absolute
full-sample estimate as its denominator; cells whose 95\% interval contains
zero are assessed from their absolute intervals instead.

\subsection{The broker primarily provides assessment, not access}

Across the simulations, the broker is the dominant channel in the market.
Principals route most demand to the broker rather than to self-search: the
outsourcing rate as a share of demand is
\pv{outBaselineLate} at the baseline (late mean, up from an early mean
of \pv{outBaselineEarly}), and it stays high across regimes (late
means of \pv{outBaseMin} to \pv{outBaseMax}). Principals prefer the broker because
its matches are better. The realized value of broker-channel matches exceeds that
of self-search matches in \pv{ogapBasePosN} of \pv{nRegimes} regimes, with
an output gap (broker mean realized output minus self-search mean realized output)
averaging $\pv{ogapBaseMean}$ across regimes (late means). This is the model's
rendering of why relational work gets outsourced: the broker constructs better
matches, on average, than clients do on their own. Table~\ref{tab:baseline-measures}
collects these measures, and the assessment measures discussed below, at the
baseline and across regimes.

The broker constructs these better matches by providing assessment,
not access. The access fraction (the share of brokered placements between two
principals with no pre-existing tie) is low, with a late mean of
\pv{accessAcrossBaseLate} across regimes (down from
\pv{accessAcrossBaseEarly} early), and it declines over time in
all regimes. Most brokered matches connect
principals who already knew each other; the broker's contribution is to identify
which of them pair well, not to bridge gaps in the network.

Moreover, the broker's assessment advantage comes from ranking candidates better,
not from accurately predicting the output of potential matches. On a held-out
sample of random partners (Appendix~A~\S8), the broker
orders prospective pairings well (rank correlation of \pv{brokerRankBaseline} with
the true ordering at the baseline, late mean, and
$\pv{brokerRankBaseMean}$ on average across regimes)
but predicts output levels poorly (holdout $R^2$ of \pv{brokerR2Baseline}
at baseline, $\pv{brokerR2BaseMean}$ on average across regimes). Principals are
weak on both, with a holdout rank correlation of \pv{agentRankBaseline} and a
holdout $R^2$ of $\pv{agentR2BaselineBase}$ (baseline, late means;
$\pv{agentRankBaseMean}$ and $\pv{agentR2BaseMean}$ on average across regimes). To pick the
best matches, the broker's services rely on a good
ordering of candidate pairings, even without an accurate appraisal of their
absolute worth.

The ordering advantage is not an artifact of neural-network flexibility. With
Ridge learning, the late broker-minus-principal rank-correlation gap is
\pv{ridgeBaselineGap} at the baseline and has a median of
\pv{ridgeMedianGap} across the \pv{ridgeNConditions} effective realizations.
The gap is positive in all \pv{ridgePositiveN} realizations. Within the
$\rho\times\delta$ design it narrows as $\delta$ increases, especially when
complementarity dominates, but remains positive at every parameter coordinate
(Supplementary Fig.~S5). Thus, within the model, a broker
using pooled mediated-match histories and an additive-plus-bilinear pair
representation does not require a neural network to rank candidates better
than principals. This result does not show that pooled data alone are
sufficient, because the Ridge broker still observes both parties and retains a
pair representation unavailable to principals.

Within the model, the broker acts not as an appraiser of general quality
(cf.\ Li~1998), but as a
matchmaker who knows which parties suit each other. Its value comes from the
ranking of complementarities, and it holds even where clients can reach
counterparties directly.

\subsection{The nature of the matching problem shapes the broker's advantage}
\label{sec:matching-shapes}

Different markets present brokers with matching problems of different kinds. In
this model, recall that $\rho$ sets the composition of the match output, from pure
general quality to pure complementarity, while $\delta$ controls the complexity of
the complementarity component.
Interestingly, across regimes, the broker's structural position tracks $\rho$
while its prediction edge tracks $\delta$, and the two need not move together.

The structural measures vary with the composition $\rho$ and are nearly flat in the
complexity $\delta$. Broker
betweenness centrality is higher where matching is more complementarity-driven
(\pv{betwRho0} at $\rho=0$ against \pv{betwRho1} at $\rho=1$; late means along the
one-at-a-time sweep, $\delta=0.5$), while at fixed $\rho=0.5$ it moves little with
the complexity of the complementarity component (\pv{betwDelta0}, \pv{betwDelta05},
\pv{betwDelta075} at
$\delta=0,0.5,0.75$). The access fraction moves the opposite way from the centrality
(\pv{accessRho0} at $\rho=0$ against \pv{accessRho1} at $\rho=1$). The
$\rho\times\eta$ grid shows the same conditional relationship at every turnover
rate: moving from $\rho=0$ to $\rho=0.85$ raises access and lowers centrality.
Under pure complementarity ($\rho=0$), the broker is more central but bridges less:
a larger share of its matches re-pair principals already tied to each other.

Meanwhile, the prediction measures vary with the complexity of the complementarity
component, $\delta$. Ordering is what the broker
needs, and its rank correlation with realized output stays high across regimes
(\pv{brokerRankD0Min} to \pv{brokerRankD0Max} on the simplest problems,
\pv{brokerRankBaseline} at baseline, falling to \pv{brokerRankHardCorner} at
$\rho=0$, $\delta=0.75$; Fig.~\ref{fig:grid}), well above the principals'
throughout (\pv{agentRankBaseline} at baseline, $\pv{agentRankBaseMean}$ on average
across regimes). Performance at predicting the
output behaves differently from ordering: the broker's holdout $R^2$ under pure
complementarity ($\rho=0$) is
$\pv{brokerR2Rho0D0}$ when the output is simple but strongly negative when it is
complex ($\pv{brokerR2Rho0D05}$ at $\delta=0.5$ and $\pv{brokerR2Rho0D075}$ at
$\delta=0.75$, late means), worse than predicting
the average and, on the hardest complementarity problems, worse than the principals
(an $R^2$ gap of $\pv{r2GapHardCorner}$ at $\rho=0$, $\delta=0.75$), despite
the broker seeing both sides of every match and pooling across the market. Ranking
which match is better withstands difficulty far better than predicting exactly how
good it will be, and the broker's ordering edge, though it narrows on the hardest
complementarity problems, is what persists across different kinds of matching
problems.

In terms of realized match quality across different matching problems, the broker
produces better matches than self-search wherever matching is
complementarity-focused, most of all where
it is also complex (the output gap is $\pv{ogapRho0OAT}$ at $\rho=0$, $\delta=0.5$,
against $\pv{ogapRho1OAT}$ at $\rho=1$; late means; Fig.~\ref{fig:grid}),
consistent with the idea that the broker matters most where match value turns on
complementarity. This follows neither structural nor prediction measures cleanly.
The broker's realized output
advantage is largest exactly in regimes where its ranking advantage over principals
is smallest,
in the hard complementarity regimes: at $\rho=0$ the rank-correlation gap is
\pv{rankGapRho0D0} at $\delta=0$ and \pv{rankGapRho0D075} at $\delta=0.75$ (grid,
late means). This is likely because in practice, picking the correct winner more
often is what really matters to realized outputs in this model, not the magnitude
of the performance gap.

\subsection{When Value Comes From Assessment, Not Access: brokers can be highly
central while doing little bridging}

In almost all regimes, the broker's structural position strengthens over time while
the agent network thins. At the baseline, mean agent degree falls
(\pv{degBaselineEarly} to \pv{degBaselineLate}, early to late means) and the
broker's betweenness centrality rises (\pv{betwBaselineEarly} to
\pv{betwBaselineLate}), and this co-movement holds in \pv{comoveN} of \pv{nRegimes}
regimes (Fig.~\ref{fig:position}). Agent turnover removes ties about as
fast as they appear, and the network does not densify: agent degree falls over time
in \pv{degFallsN} of \pv{nRegimes} regimes. This raises a crucial question:
why is the structural advantage not self-liquidating, even at low turnover (at
$\eta=0.01$, betweenness centrality still rises from \pv{betwEta001Early} to
\pv{betwEta001Late})?

Assessment and access have opposite effects on the broker's structural position.
The broker lies on the shortest path between clients and roster members who are not
directly connected. An assessment match pairs principals who already have a tie,
so it does not add a direct path or eliminate the broker's position between other
agents. An access match creates a new agent-to-agent tie. For that pair, the broker
ceases to be the shortest connection. Assessment therefore allows the broker to
serve the market without eroding the network structure that makes it central,
whereas access consumes that structural opportunity.

Turnover replenishes structural opportunity. It removes agents and their
accumulated ties, then introduces entrants without established connections. The
$\rho\times\eta$ grid separates this effect from the composition of the matching
problem (Fig.~\ref{fig:position}). At every $\rho$, increasing turnover raises both
the access fraction and broker centrality. At every turnover rate, moving from
$\rho=0$ to $\rho=0.85$ raises access but lowers centrality. Turnover and matching
composition therefore generate different relationships between access and
centrality: turnover recreates gaps in the network, while movement toward general
quality makes the broker's work more likely to fill those gaps with direct ties.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figs/fig3_position_work.png}
\caption{\textbf{\pvtitle{position}.} \pvcaption{position}}
\label{fig:position}
\end{figure}

The pure-quality boundary ($\rho=1$) isolates the endpoint of this relationship.
Principals there match well on their own, outsourcing is somewhat lower
(\pv{outRho1Group} against \pv{outRho0Group} at $\rho=0$, late means), and brokered
matches are twice as often access (\pv{accessRho1Group} against
\pv{accessRho0Group}). Broker centrality is nevertheless far lower, with a late
mean of \pv{betwRho1Group} across $\rho=1$ regimes against
\pv{betwBaselineLate} at baseline. Higher turnover raises both access and
centrality within the pure-quality boundary, but centrality remains below that of
the complementarity-heavy regimes at the same turnover rate. The broker does not
begin highly central and then lose its position as access ties accumulate. It
never accumulates a comparable position. Within runs, the access share still
declines, and the network thins in \pv{rhoOneThinN} of \pv{rhoOneN} pure-quality
regimes.

The broker can therefore be highly central while doing little bridging, but low
access alone does not make it central. With little turnover, principals retain
their accumulated ties, and both access and broker centrality remain low. With
moderate or high turnover, complementarity-heavy regimes combine renewed gaps in
the network with brokerage that primarily assesses existing relationships. These
are the regimes in which the broker becomes most central. Moving toward general
quality makes brokered matches more likely to provide access, creating direct ties
that leave the broker less central. High centrality thus requires both a continuing
supply of structural gaps and brokerage that fills requested positions mainly
through assessment. Because access remains low overall (a late mean of
\pv{accessAcrossBaseLate} across regimes and declining within runs), the broker's
work does little to eliminate the structural basis of its own position.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth]{figs/fig4_advantage.png}
\caption{\textbf{\pvtitle{advantage}.} \pvcaption{advantage}}
\label{fig:advantage}
\end{figure}

Across effective realizations (late means), the broker's output advantage is
greatest in the complementarity-heavy regimes where it is most central and provides
relatively little access (Fig.~\ref{fig:advantage}). This pooled association is
driven by the composition of the matching problem, not by a uniformly negative
relationship between access and centrality. Turnover raises access and centrality
together, while movement toward general quality raises access and lowers
centrality. Complementarity-dominated regimes ($\rho=0$) are sparse and
brokered-assessment-heavy: principals hold fewer ties, outsource more of their
demand, and the broker is at once most central and most valuable while providing
the least access (Table~\ref{tab:rhogroups}; Fig.~\ref{fig:advantage}).
Quality-dominated regimes ($\rho=1$) sit at the other end of each of these
measures. Structural opportunity and broker value accumulate together where
turnover renews network gaps and matching depends on complementarity.
